coredata.dc:description: An effective strategy to improve both the conductivity and alkaline stability of anion exchange membranes (AEMs) was proposed by incorporating quaternary ammonium functionalized polyhedral oligomeric silsesquioxane (QPOSS) into quaternized poly(2,6-dimethyl-1,4-phenylene oxide) (QPPO). Glycidyltrimethylammonium chloride (GTMAC) was used as the main quaternized reagent for the synthesis of QPOSS. The introduction of QPOSS provided the hybrid membranes with additional ion hopping sites and ion conducting channels. The QPPO-QPOSS membrane with high ion exchange capacity of 4.81 meq g−1 possessed the hydroxide ion conductivity of 8.77 × 10−2 Scm−1 at 80 °C. Meanwhile, the hybrid composite membranes showed enhanced alkaline stability due to the steric hindrance offered by QPPO and QPOSS and good alkaline resistance of long alkyl chain from octaammonium and glycidyl trimethyl ammonium bulky substituents. The residual ratio of hydroxide conductivity of QPPO-QPOSS-3 after being treated with 1 M KOH at room temperature for 1200 h reached 102%. The improved interfacial compatibility among the matrix polymer and filler imparted the hybrid membranes enhanced mechanical properties, good dimensional and thermal stability. The H2/O2 fuel cell using composite membrane of 3 wt% QPOSS relative to QPPO reached a maximum power density of about 288 mWcm−2. The prepared hybrid membrane with promising characteristics exhibited the potential for applications in alkaline anion exchange membrane fuel cells in considering their integrative properties.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: An effective strategy to improve both the conductivity and alkaline stability of anion exchange membranes (AEMs) was proposed by incorporating quaternary ammonium functionalized polyhedral oligomeric silsesquioxane (QPOSS) into quaternized poly(2,6-dimethyl-1,4-phenylene oxide) (QPPO). Glycidyltrimethylammonium chloride (GTMAC) was used as the main quaternized reagent for the synthesis of QPOSS. The introduction of QPOSS provided the hybrid membranes with additional ion hopping sites and ion conducting channels. The QPPO-QPOSS membrane with high ion exchange capacity of 4.81 meq g−1 possessed the hydroxide ion conductivity of 8.77 × 10−2 Scm−1 at 80 °C. Meanwhile, the hybrid composite membranes showed enhanced alkaline stability due to the steric hindrance offered by QPPO and QPOSS and good alkaline resistance of long alkyl chain from octaammonium and glycidyl trimethyl ammonium bulky substituents. The residual ratio of hydroxide conductivity of QPPO-QPOSS-3 after being treated with 1 M KOH at room temperature for 1200 h reached 102%. The improved interfacial compatibility among the matrix polymer and filler imparted the hybrid membranes enhanced mechanical properties, good dimensional and thermal stability. The H2/O2 fuel cell using composite membrane of 3 wt% QPOSS relative to QPPO reached a maximum power density of about 288 mWcm−2. The prepared hybrid membrane with promising characteristics exhibited the potential for applications in alkaline anion exchange membrane fuel cells in considering their integrative properties.

ce:section.ce:para: The increasing demand for high quality and clean energy directed towards the development of fuel cells as environmentally friendly power source and alternative for conventional fossil fuel processes [1,2]. Among various types, alkaline anion exchange membrane fuel cells (AEMFCs) due to their significant advantages of faster oxygen reduction kinetics at high pH conditions, reduced dependence on noble metal catalysts and reduction in membrane cost have elicited considerable attention nowadays [3,4]. Unfortunately, the most current anion exchange membranes (AEMs), the main parts of alkaline fuel cells, faces a trade-off between conductivity, dimensional and chemical stabilities under alkaline conditions especially at higher temperature [5,6]. The AEMs with high ion exchange capacity usually exhibited high water uptake and poor dimensional stability which can affect the continuous and stable operation of AEMFCs [7]. Therefore, controlling the swelling and long term alkaline stability is critical to improve the performance properties of the fuel cells.

The use of organic-inorganic hybrid composites came up as a remarkable revolution to improve the stability of membranes due to the combined merits of organic and inorganic individual components [8]. The inorganic filler increases the hydrophilicity of the membrane by absorbing water molecules and facilitating ion exchange by diffusion mechanism. Moreover, the physical/chemical bonding among filler and polymer can improve thermal and mechanical behaviours [9]. Polyhedral oligomeric silsesquioxanes (POSS), a kind of organic-inorganic hybrid materials, possess a unique cage-like structure with nano scale dimensions (1–3 nm dia) and environmental neutrality, good thermal stability and excellent thermo oxidative stability. Compared to other inorganic doped particles, POSS has many surface functional alkyl groups, which can be modified through covalent or non-covalent approaches to improve the physical and chemical properties [10–13]. Therefore, pristine POSS and modified POSS have been investigated in AEMFC membranes, but to a much lesser extent. Li and his co-workers recently incorporated imidazolium functionalized octaphenyl polyhedral oligomeric silsesquioxane into imidazolium functionalized poly(ether ether ketone) (ImPEEK), obtaining a well-defined microstructure which promoted fast ionic mobility [14]. Miao et al. functionalized POSS with glycidylammonium chloride and composited with quaternized polysulfone (QPSU) exhibited 60% improvement in conductivity at 80 °C than that of pure QPSU and retained about 50% of conductivity for composite with 3% QPOSS even after treated with 1 M KOH solution [13].

The insufficient stability of quaternary ammonium groups against hydroxide attack due to nucleophilic substitution, Hofmann and (or) E1 elimination reaction especially at higher temperature limited its application. The use of long alkyl chain and hence the steric hindrance generated reduces the possibility of Hofmann elimination and nucleophilic substitution reaction and was found to exhibit good conductivity and excellent alkaline stability [15,16]. Inspired by these attractive features, octaammonium POSS having relatively long alkyl chain in the structure with quaternary ammonium group was synthesized in this work to promote ion conductivity even after prolonged alkaline exposure.

The present work focused on the improvement of transport properties and alkaline stability of anion exchange membranes based on trimethylamine functionalized poly(2,6-dimethyl-1,4-phenylene oxide) (QPPO) while preserving an acceptable swelling ratio by incorporating quaternized octa ammonium POSS (QPOSS). Poly(2,6-dimethyl-1,4-phenylene oxide) has excellent mechanical properties and high thermal and chemical stability [17]. In this study, we have synthesized QPPO and QPOSS and subsequently the novel organic – inorganic QPPO-QPOSS hybrid composite membranes were prepared using solvent casting technique.

Scrutiny of the available literature reveals that there is no report available on QPPO-QPOSS hybrid composite electrolyte membranes for alkaline anion exchange membrane fuel cell applications (AEMFCs). The glycidyltrimethylammonium chloride (GDTMAC) functionalized OPOSS rendered the QPPO membrane with high ion exchange capacity coupled with acceptable swelling and excellent alkaline stability. The influence of the QPOSS on hydroxide conductivity, water uptake, mechanical and thermal properties of the membranes were also discussed in detail.

poly(2,6-dimethyl-1,4-phenylene oxide) (PPO, Mw: about 50000 g mol−1 using GPC) was purchased from Asahi Kasei, Japan. Octaammonium polyhedral oligomeric silsesquioxanes (OPOSS) was obtained from hybrid plastics. Glycidyltrimethylammonium chloride (GDTMAC, > 90%), 2,2’ – azobis-isobutyronitrile (AIBN, 12 wt% in acetone), N – bromosuccinimide (NBS, 99%), triethylamine, trimethylamine and dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) were supplied by Sigma Aldrich. Chloro benzene (99%) and N – methyl – 2- pyrrolidone (NMP, 99%) were procured from Samchun chemicals, Korea. All other chemicals were obtained from commercial sources and are used as received without further purification.

The synthetic method of QPPO is shown in Scheme 1 [18]. PPO (5 g) was dissolved in chlorobenzene (86 mL) at 60 °C by continuous stirring (~2 h) under nitrogen atmosphere. After complete dissolution, 2,2’ – azobis-isobutyronitrile (AIBN) (0.05 g) and N – bromosuccinimide (NBS) (3.70 g) were added and the reaction mixture was refluxed at 135 °C for 3 h. After that, the reaction mixture was cooled to room temperature and precipitated in excess of methanol. The precipitate obtained was then filtered, washed repeatedly with methanol and dried in vacuum oven at 60 °C for 24 h to produce the bromo methylated PPO (Br-PPO). The quaternization of Br-PPO was carried out using 45 wt% trimethylamine (TMA) solution. TMA (5.78 mL) was added after complete dissolution of Br-PPO (5 g) in NMP (86 mL) and continued the reaction for 48 h at 60 °C followed by precipitation in ethyl acetate. The precipitate collected was then dried at 60 °C for 24 h in a vacuum oven. The degree of quaternization was calculated using 1H NMR spectroscopy.

Quaternized octaammonium POSS (QPOSS) was synthesized according to the literature published elsewhere with some modification (Scheme 2 ) [13]. 0.69 g octaammonium POSS (OPOSS) was mixed with triethylamine (0.25 mL) and 35 mL tetrahydrofuran in a two necked round bottom flask equipped with a magnetic bar under nitrogen atmosphere. After stirring for 15 min, 2.48 g GTMAC was added and continued stirring for 1 h at 35 °C and then for 4 h at 60 °C. The reaction mixture was then cooled to room temperature and precipitated using ethyl acetate. The mixture was centrifuged, filtered and the product obtained was washed several times with isopropanol and dried at 60 °C under vacuum for 12 h.

The composite membranes were prepared by using solvent casting technique. 0.25 g QPPO dissolved in 5 mL NMP and various percentages of QPOSS (1, 3 and 5 wt % of QPPO) in 5 mL DMSO was mixed together for 4 h at room temperature. The obtained mixture was cast onto a clear glass Petri dish and then successfully dried at 60 °C for 12 h under vacuum. The obtained hybrid composite membranes were peeled off from the Petri dishes and immersed in 1 M KOH solution for 24 h to obtain the quaternized membrane in OH− form. After that the membranes were washed with de-ionized water until the rinse solution became neutral to remove the residual KOH, and dried at room temperature for 24 h. The produced membranes with thickness in the range of 20–30 μm were named QPPO-QPOSS-X, where X represented the weight percentage of the filler to the polymer (X = 1, 3 and 5). Polymer membrane without QPOSS was also prepared as control sample (QPPO). The photographs of QPPO-QPOSS membranes are presented in supplementary information (Fig. S1).

The Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) analysis was conducted with Nicolet impact 400, thermo scientific spectrometer equipped with ZnSe crystal in the spectral range from 4000 to 600 cm−1 with a 4 cm−1 resolution in 64 scans to confirm quaternization and formation of the composites. Successful formation of QPPO and QPOSS was also confirmed by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (1H NMR, DRX-300, Bruker). The surface and cross sectional morphology and elemental mapping of QPPO-QPOSS composite membranes were analyzed using a field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, Philips XL 30S FEG) equipped with an EDAX detector after subjecting the samples for gold sputtering. Mechanical properties of the membranes were studied using a universal testing machine (UTM, LR10K, Lloyd Instrument) at a cross head speed of 10 mm min−1. The thermal stability of membranes in the OH− form was evaluated on a thermogravimetric analyzer (TGA Q50, TA Instrument) operating from 30 °C to 800 °C under nitrogen atmosphere at a heating rate of 10 °C min−1. Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC Q 20, TA instrument) (DSC) was used to determine the melting temperatures and enthalpy of transitions of the membranes. The experiment consists of two heating runs, first from 30 to 250 °C and second from 30 to 350 °C at a heating and cooling rate of 10 °C min−1 under nitrogen atmosphere.

The state of water in the membranes was determined by heating the hydrated membranes using thermogravimetric analyzer at a heating rate of 10 °C min−1 under nitrogen atmosphere [20]. The weight loss above 100 °C is due to the loss of water, which is tightly bound to the ionic sites in the membranes. The resistance of the composite membranes to alkaline environment was estimated based on the change of ion conductivities after being immersed in 1 M KOH solution at room temperature for 1200 h. The conductivity was measured at 80 °C in deionized water. Original anionic conductivity of the membranes (σinitial) in OH− form was measured. The residual ratio of hydroxide ion conductivity was also calculated and recorded (σ/σinitial). The stability in terms of weight loss was also studied using different concentrations of KOH solutions. The dried composite membranes (60 °C for 24 h) were immersed in various molar concentrations of KOH solutions for specified time duration and weighed after drying at 60 °C for 24 h.

Single cell performance using the membranes were analyzed at 60 °C under 100% RH and H2 and O2 fed flow rates of 200 cm3 min−1 and 400 cm3 min−1 respectively. The catalyst inks were prepared by ultra-sonicating a mixture of Pt/C catalysts (Tanaka, 46.2 wt%), deionized water, 1-propanol and ionomer solution (Fumatech, Fumion FAA – 3, 10 wt% in NMP). The CCMs (Catalyst Coated Membranes) were prepared by coating the inks on the membrane (0.4 mg Pt/cm2) with an air spray gun. The membrane electrode assembly (MEA) was sandwiched between gas diffusion layers (GDL, Sigracet 39 BCE) and gaskets (Teflon®) and the effective electrode area was 5 cm2.

The bromination and quaternization reactions were confirmed by using 1H NMR spectra (Fig. 1 ). The shift at 6.4–6.8 ppm is assigned to the aryl protons of PPO. The proton corresponding to the benzyl group appeared at 1.92–2.25 ppm (Fig. 1(a)) [21]. The bromination transpires exclusively at the benzylic position of PPO and the sharp peak observed at around 4.27 ppm confirmed the successful formation of brominated PPO (Br-PPO) (Fig. 1(b)) [22]. The degree of bromination was estimated using 1H NMR spectra from the integral area ratio of aryl proton peaks (Ar–H) (ppm) (a and b in Fig. 1(b)) as 35%. As shown in Fig. 1(c), the small shifting of the peak corresponding to methylene peak (-CH2Br) towards 4.5 ppm and the appearance of a sharp new chemical shift corresponding to the protons on trimethylammonium cations at around 3.2 ppm indicates the successful quaternization and the degree of substitution obtained was about 37%.

In addition, the chemical structure of the functionalized PPO was also supported by FTIR spectroscopy (Fig. 2 ). The band observed at 1600 cm−1 corresponds to C=C bond stretching and the peak at 1190 cm−1 is due to the C–O–C stretching of PPO [23]. The stretching vibration bands (C–Br) observed at 730 cm−1 and 1080 cm−1 in Br-PPO confirm the bromination of PPO [21,24]. After quaternization of Br-PPO using TMA, the peak at 730 cm−1 was disappeared and a new band assigned to N–H stretch was aroused near 3325 cm−1 which confirmed that the –CH2Br group is converted to –N+(CH3)3 group [22].

In the FTIR spectrum of OPOSS, NH3 + stretching and bending vibrations are observed at 3430 cm−1 and 1610 cm−1 respectively [25]. The peaks at 1225 cm−1, 1080 cm−1 and 705 cm−1 are due to the existence of C–N stretching, Si–O–Si symmetric stretching and Si–C stretching respectively [13]. The absorption peaks at 2810 cm−1 and 2897 cm−1 are assigned to C–H stretching of methoxy and methylene groups respectively [9]. In QPOSS, the absorption band with moderate intensity observed at 1475 cm−1 is attributed to the symmetric stretching of N–C bond in quaternary ammonium group [9]. Moreover, the peak correspond to NH3 + bending has been shifted to 1580 cm−1 after reacting with glycidyltrimethylammonium chloride and a new peak belongs to the quaternary ammonium group appeared at 1738 cm−1 indicating that the nano cage like OPOSS material was successfully grafted with quaternary ammonium groups.

In order to bring about a new generation of PPO based hybrid AEMs with excellent alkaline stability and good hydroxide ion conductivity, we designed a series of quaternary ammonium functionalized PPO/glycidyltrimethylammonium functionalized POSS based hybrid composites in which the presence of long alkyl chain grafted on the inorganic material is expected to increase the durability of the resulting AEMs. Various literatures reported indicated that, increasing the chain length or size of alkyl substituents in quaternary ammonium ions can increase the electrochemical stability of those ions and hence the membranes [15,16]. The reason for good stability was explained by the higher blocking and shielding effect as well as increased electron donating characteristics of larger alkyl groups. The steric hindrance offered by the alkyl chains can protect the organic cations from being attacked by hydroxide ions, which improves the stability. The substituent groups with electron donating effect can increase the electron density on the cation site, depressing the electrostatic attraction, which help stabilizing the cations. The structure of QPPO-QPOSS composite membranes with varying percentages of QPOSS was investigated by FTIR analysis. The FTIR spectra of QPPO-QPOSS composite membranes are shown in Fig. 5 , where the broad band at around 3500 cm−1 is assigned to the stretching vibration of O–H and the band at 1020 cm−1 correspond to the C–OH stretching vibrations respectively [26]. The bands at 1460 cm−1 and 1600 cm−1 are belongs to the characteristic CH2 bending and C=C stretching of phenyl group and the peak at 1190 cm−1 is due to C–O–C stretching of PPO respectively [27]. In addition, the band at 1300 cm−1 belongs to the quaternization of PPO (C–N stretching) [28]. The new absorption band at 1688 cm−1 in all the membranes other than the pristine QPPO membrane corresponding to the quaternary ammonium functionalization of QPOSS indicate the formation of hybrid composite membranes.

The surface and internal microstructure of the composite membranes were further studied using field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) and the resulting images are presented in Fig. S2 & Fig. S3 respectively. The absence of any obvious defects such as pin - holes, cracks and pores on the freeze fractured cross section of AEMs shows the homogeneity and compatibility between the polymer and the filler [8]. The similar quaternary ammonium groups belonging to both QPPO and GDTMAC contributed to the compatibility and homogeneous distribution of QPOSS. The improved compatibility among QPOSS and the matrix polymer is beneficial to the formation of long range ion conduction channels. However, a minimum visible aggregations and roughness were observed on the surface of the membrane possessing highest content of QPOSS, which might block the ion transport channels (Fig. S2 (d)). In the compositional mapping images of the pristine QPPO, QPPO-QPOSS-3 and QPPO-QPOSS-5 membrane surfaces (Fig. S4), Si element distribution confirms the dispersion of filler on the surface of the membranes. Besides, to prove the homogeneity of the composite membranes, EDAX elemental mapping of QPPO and QPPO-QPOSS-3 cross – section was also investigated. Fig. S5 (a and b) shows the element mapping in the cross – section which can confirm the homogeneous structure of the composite membrane.

The thermal stability of the QPPO-QPOSS composite membranes were evaluated using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and the weight loss as a function of temperature is illustrated in Fig. 6 . All the composite membranes show three main stages of decomposition. The primordial degradation below 230 °C with weight loss of 6–12% attributes to the evaporation of absorbed/bound water and residual solvent present in the membranes. The second weight loss from 230 °C to 350 °C belongs to the cleavage of quaternary ammonium group present in the membranes. The final weight loss above 350 °C is due to the degradation of polymer backbone [27,29]. The thermal decomposition from 100 to 450 °C has been highlighted in Fig. S6. The thermal decomposition of composites from 100 °C to 230 °C is due to the combined effect of water and solvent absorbed which is very less in quantity and therefore, looks quite similar. Excluding the decomposition occurring up to 230 °C, the thermal stability of the composites improved through the addition of QPOSS nanoparticles below 450 °C which can be ascribed to the strong interfacial interactions among the filler particles and polymer matrix. The hydrophilic interactions (physical interactions) from the quaternary groups of polymer and filler are believed to be responsible for the improved performance of the membranes. However, the percentage improvement is not pronounced in composite membranes with increase in QPOSS content. 3 wt% loading is the optimum dosage, above which the filler has no effect on the thermal stability of the membrane due to its poor dispersion. Moreover, compared with the pristine membrane, the composite membranes showed more weight loss at high temperature. This may be attributed to the decomposition of QPOSS which had lower thermal stability than that of polymer main chains at high temperature within the composite membranes. The same behavior of degradation has also been reported in quaternized polyhedral oligomeric silsesquioxanes modified polysulfone based composite anion exchange membranes [13]. All the prepared membranes exhibited thermal decomposition temperature higher than 200 °C, suggesting its sufficient thermal stability suitable for application in fuel cells that operates at below 100 °C [30].

Fig. 7 shows the DSC thermograms in nitrogen environment of the representative composite membranes with varying QPOSS content. As observed in the first heating curves, the desorption of weakly bonded molecules takes place at around 100 °C, however strongly bonded molecules are released at temperature around 170 °C. A small shoulder also appeared at around 190 °C due to the loss of solvent molecules present in the membranes. The glass transition of the polymers is normally observed as gradual increase in the heat capacity of the sample during heating, due to the enhanced molecular motion in the polymer. In the second heating, no endothermic peaks corresponding to Tg of QPPO observed for the membranes at any temperature up to 250 °C. This may be due to the enhanced molecular interactions among QPPO polymer backbones owing to its relatively little steric hindrance caused by the quaternary ammonium groups [18]. In addition QPPO-QPOSS composite membranes showed a melting temperature (Tm) with an endotherm assigned at about 285 °C. A closer look at Fig. 7 (b) reveals a reduction in the intensity and peak area with QPOSS content up to 3 wt% loading which indicates the decrease in crystallinity of the composites with increasing filler content. This may be due to the physical and molecular changes caused by the interaction among polymer and filler which suggest the formation of more stable membranes.

The excellent mechanical stability of anion exchange membranes is crucial for the durability and performance of fuel cells. The mechanical performance of the dried membranes in OH− form is summarized in Table 1 . From Table 1, it can be seen that the pristine QPPO membrane showed a tensile strength of 9.3 MPa and elongation at break of 25.3%. It is worth to note that the tensile strength of the membranes increased with increasing QPOSS up to 3 wt%. On the contrary, the trend of elongation is opposite ascribed that the higher loading of filler resulted in increased stiffness and reduced flexibility of the membranes attributed to the restricted movement of polymer chains caused by the interfacial interaction among the polymer and filler [31]. The maximum tensile strength of 15.4 MPa with the breaking elongation of 18.8% was achieved for QPPO-QPOSS-3 membrane. Further addition of QPOSS lead to the reduction of mechanical strength as the homogeneity of the membranes destroyed by the aggregate of nano filler. At higher filler loading, due to improper dispersion or clustering all filler particles are not able to be wetted by the polymer chains means not attached to the polymer chains. Thus loose filler cluster can act as the stress concentration points under applied stress from where the crack initiation starts leading to composite failure. In brief, the above results indicate that the composite membranes possess good mechanical strength which could meet the application requirements.

ce:section.ce:section-title: Water uptake, dimensional stability, state of water and ion exchange capacity
ce:section.ce:para: The water uptake and swelling behavior (dimensional stability) of the membranes are shown in Fig. 8 and ion exchange capacity is summarized in Table 1. Even though the water as media facilitates transport of charge carriers, excess water results in loss of mechanical stability and even a drop in ionic conductivity. An ideal AEM should retain proper water uptake, mechanical properties and excellent conductivity [2,30]. As shown in Fig. 8 (a and b), the water content has a great influence on the swelling behavior of the membrane. The water uptake and longitudinal swelling percentage of QPPO-QPOSS-3 (WU = 8.1%; Swelling = 6.3%) are higher than that of QPPO-QPOSS-1 (WU = 6.7%; Swelling = 5.3%) and QPPO-QPOSS-5 (WU = 7.9%; Swelling = 5.2%) membranes. Moreover, these values are comparatively less than that of QPPO membrane (WU = 17.4%; Swelling = 7.2%) which displays its better stability. The increased hydrophilicity is owing to the presence of large number of –N+(CH3)3 groups in the membrane at higher concentration of QPOSS. Furthermore, the grafting of GTMAC can decrease the crystallinity of POSS which may leads to the drop in crystallinity of the hybrid composite membranes. These together attributed to the water – membrane interaction and high absorption of water up to 3 wt% filler loading. Fig. 8 (a and b) shows the temperature dependence on water uptake and dimensional stability of QPPO-QPOSS membranes in hydroxide form. As expected, the water uptake and swelling percentage increased with temperature. This may be attributed to the increased mobility of the polymer chains at elevated temperature to provide more space for holding water [32]. The in-plane swelling of QPPO-QPOSS-3 membrane is found to be 2.3 times lower than that of pure QPPO membrane at 80 °C showed its improvement in dimensional stability.

IEC is defined as the number of milli equivalents of ion exchangeable sites present in 1 g of the membrane. As the QPOSS content increased to 3 wt%, IEC of the membranes in OH− form also increased from 2.33 meq g−1 for pristine QPPO membrane (2.45 meq g−1 theoretical IEC) to 4.81 meq g−1 due to the large amount of hydroxide ion clusters formed in quaternized POSS structure as every single QPOSS molecule contains eight quaternary ammonium ion exchange groups [9]. On the other hand, when the quantity of QPOSS was too high resulting a decrease in the IEC value. In general, the higher the IEC values, the higher the water uptake and swelling. However, the structural design and morphology of the membrane has a critical effect on the water absorption in the AEMs. In the present work, when the QPOSS content in the membrane increase from 0 to 1 wt%, water uptake decreased from 17.4% to 6.7% and IEC increased from 2.33 to 3.95 meq g−1 attributed to the presence of Si–O–Si network in the membrane and reduction in void volume and hence comparatively lower rate of water diffusion. IEC and water uptake are progressively increased as the content of QPOSS further increased up to 3 wt% because water molecules tend to associate with the charged functional (quaternary ammonium) groups. However, the aggregation and blocking of ion exchangeable sites impeded ion exchange process during titration and reduction in the number of polar groups available for water absorption and decrease in free volume causes reduction in IEC and water uptake at higher concentration of filler [33,34].

To further elucidate the swelling behavior, the state of water was calculated using TGA and the results are illustrated in Fig. 8 (c) and Table 1. The main types of water present in membranes are of two types – free and bound water. Free water can populate ion conduction channels and bound water forms the ion solvent shell [16]. Bound water is more responsible for ionic conduction at higher temperature as it is not easily evaporating than bulk/free water. QPPO-QPOSS-5 shows the highest bound water content (2.26%) among all the membranes under discussion. However, its bulk water is lower compared to QPPO-QPOSS-3 membrane due to the inadequate free space as a result of filler agglomeration. This observation is also supported by FESEM analysis. The presence of high bulk water (15.72%) and low bound water (1.68%) resulted in decreased conductivity (18.4 mS cm−1 at 80 °C) for pristine QPPO membrane. The lower free water (4.99%) for QPPO-QPOSS-1 membrane was also not sufficient to support effective ion transport. The ion conductivity observed was about 33.8 mS cm−1 at 80 °C. Higher conductivity was observed for QPPPO-QPOSS-3 membrane (71.3 mS cm−1 at 80 °C) with bound and bulk/free water of 1.75% and 6.35% respectively. Hence the best balance among both bound and bulk water is required to support effective ion transport, which is also supported by the study conducted by Mandal et al. [16].

Ionic conductivity of the OH− form membrane is an important parameter affecting the performance of AEMs, which has a profound impact on the practical application in fuel cells [35]. Ionic conductivity of the membranes can be affected by many factors, such as the polymer structure/chain mobility, compatibility among filler/dopant and polymer, water uptake, ion concentration and mobility [36]. It can be seen from Fig. 9 that the hydroxide ion conductivity of the composite membranes in deionized water was obviously improved with the increasing content of QPOSS as compared with that of pristine membrane. In particular, QPPO-QPOSS-3 membrane showed 327% improvement in the hydroxide ion conductivity than that of the pristine QPPO membrane and reached the highest value of 5.12 × 10−2 Scm−1 at room temperature attributed to the high density of ion exchangeable groups and surface area of the nano fillers, that would provide less resistance for hydroxyl ion movement [9]. The presence of flexible alkyl side chains on OPOSS along with the glycidyltrimethylammonium chloride promote the formation of the distinct hydrophilic/hydrophobic micro phase separation in the hybrid composite membranes. The connected hydrophilic regions provide continuous OH− ion conduction channels in the membranes. Moreover, the nano particles may interrupt the QPPO crystallite alignment, resulting more amorphous regions and paths for ion conduction through the electrolyte. The change in structural arrangements has also been supported by the DSC results. In addition, as reported in other literatures, the conductivity of all the composite membranes also increased with temperature over the range of 25–80 °C due to the increasing free volume of the composite membranes through the mobility of QPPO chains and hence accelerated diffusion of ionic clusters at high temperature [30,37]. QPPO-QPOSS-3 membrane exhibited a conductivity of 8.77 × 10−2 Scm−1 at 80 °C shows its good water retention ability as discussed in the state of water section and decreased distance among the functional ammonium groups [38,39]. All the prepared composite membranes showed ion conductivity above 10 mS cm−1 over the whole temperature range, which is the basic requirement for the working of fuel cells [24]. At QPOSS concentration exceed 3 wt%, the more compact structure of the membrane lead to increasing tortuosity, which weakens anion transport in the composite membranes [40]. The ionic conductivity shows the same trend in line with the IEC. Compare to the composite membranes, pristine QPPO membrane showed maximum water uptake but lower conductivity which implies the higher dependence of the ion exchangeable sites in the conductivity. Table S1 shows the comparative study of conductivity values of QPPO-QPOSS-3 membrane in the present work with different AEMs reported in various literatures. As a matter of fact, the membrane in the present work is in the top rank of OH− conductivity compared to the other membranes.

Fig. 9 (b) demonstrates the Arrhenius plot for the estimation of activation energy (Ea) required for hydroxide ion conduction across the membrane. The ion conductivity of the membranes followed an Arrhenius behavior. Activation energy was calculated using the slope of the regression line of ln σ vs. 1000/T (°K−1) as per the Arrhenius equation published elsewhere [41]. The values are 9.15 KJ mol−1, 7.17 KJ mol−1, 8.56 KJ mol−1 and 9.0 KJ mol−1 respectively for QPPO, QPPO-QPOSS-1, QPPO-QPOSS-3 and QPPO-QPOSS-5. Activation energy of the composite membranes are lower than that of the pristine QPPO membrane which demonstrate the need for less energy in composite membrane due to the contribution of ionizable groups from nano particles for conduction [42]. The presence of more quaternary ammonium groups in the composites can contribute additional continuous ion conducting channels for hydroxide transportation and impart higher conductivity and lower activation energy [24]. The Ea values are in the range of 9.15–7.17 KJ mol−1. These values are comparatively better than those values of previously reported alkaline membranes (18-12 KJ mol−1 for PPO/Silica [36], 12–15 KJ mol−1 for PPO/IL-GO [29], 17–22 KJ mol−1 for ImPES [43] and 12.75 KJ mol−1 for Nafion – 117 [44] membranes). The well linear fit acquired in conductivity indicate that the mechanism of conduction is primarily governed by Grotthuss/hopping of conducting species.

To further explore the reliability of the prepared hybrid membranes, the change in hydroxide conductivity of the aged membranes (1 M KOH solution at room temperature) at 80 °C was recorded as a function of time in Fig. 10 (a). All the pristine and composite membranes exhibited improvement in conductivity even after the alkaline treatment for 200 h indicating the absence of polymer chain scission during that period. The absorbed KOH solution might be well confined inside the ionic channels and the OH− cations could be better solvated in deionized water and participated in conduction and hence retarded the decomposition of quaternary ammonium groups [34]. All the prepared membranes exhibited reduction in conductivity over time only after 200 h of chemical exposure. However, the values are not less than the initial conductivity even after 1200 h indicating the excellent alkaline stability of the membranes. The improved chemical stability could be attributed to the steric hindrance offered by the ammonium group of QPPO and grafted long alkyl chain (glycidyl trimethyl ammonium and octaammonium) in QPOSS. The steric hindrance offered by the bulky substituents of QPOSS reducing the access of nucleophilic attack to the quaternary ammonium groups by the excess amount of OH− [34].

Fig. 10 (b) shows the percentage of initial conductivity value vs. exposure time of the membranes. After 1200 h of exposure, the conductivity of QPPO, QPPO-QPOSS-1, QPPO-QPOSS-3 and QPPO-QPOSS-5 increased by 148%, 199%, 2% and 10% respectively of their initial values. Low IEC values accompanying with low water uptake may be the factors responsible for high alkaline stability of membranes at lower filler loading The increased number of functional group/IEC may intensify the hydroxyl attack and which may be the reason leading to the drop in alkaline stability retention at higher filler content observed [48–50]. The effect of IEC and water uptake on alkaline stability has also been reported by Zhang and his co-workers in their work [48]. The alkaline stability of QPPO-QPOSS membranes was compared with that of other quaternary ammonium (QA) based AEMs reported in the literatures (illustrated in Table S1). The hybrid AEMs in the present work showed competitive alkaline resistance. On the basis of the abovementioned findings, we can confirm that the hybrid AEMs in this work exhibited excellent alkaline stability than the other reported membranes and could be capable of withstanding OH− attack during the long term operation of fuel cells.

QPPO-QPOSS - 3 was selected for H2/O2 single cell alkaline exchange membrane fuel cell testing because of its overall best performance and compared with the performance of pristine QPPO membrane. The fuel cell was operated at 60 °C as many other AEMFCs found in literature. The cell performance was recorded under the operation condition that H2/O2 were fed with a flow rate of 200/400 cm3min-1 and 100% RH. As seen in Fig. 11 , a peak power density of 288 mWcm−2 was obtained for QPPO-QPOSS-3 at 0.43 V and current density of 662 mAcm−2. The corresponding value of QPPO was 259 mWcm−2 at 0.40 V and 642 mAcm−2. It is worth to note that higher OCVs of 0.96 V was observed for 3 wt% QPOSS filled membrane. The high power density obtained in the composite membrane was on par with the previous literatures [33,51]. The additional quaternary ammonium based ion exchange groups present in the QPOSS facilitates the hydroxyl ion conductivity via both Grotthus (through hydrogen bond networks of water molecules) as well as diffusion mechanisms, strongly suggesting that the newly developed system has the possibility of improving the performance of the fuel cell.

A series of hybrid composite anion exchange membranes based on quaternized PPO and quaternized POSS were prepared with solution casting technique followed by hydroxide exchange in potassium hydroxide solution. To the author's knowledge, this is the first anion exchange membrane based on quaternized poly(2,6-dimethyl-1,4-phenylene oxide) (QPPO)/glycidyltrimethylammonium chloride grafted octaammonium polyhedral oligomeric silsesquioxane (QPOSS). These membranes displayed an application stability up to 230 °C without any degradation of cationic groups and polymer backbone. The newly prepared QPPO-QPOSS membrane with an IEC of 4.81 meq g−1 exhibited a conductivity of 8.77 × 10−2 Scm−1 at 80 °C shows its good water retention ability. Water content in QPPO-QPOSS-3 was measured using TGA analysis and it was found that 6.35% unbound/bulk water and 1.75% bound water molecules in the membrane leading to the best ion conductivity among all the fabricated membranes. Furthermore, the membrane showed 102% of the initial conductivity at 80 °C even after 1200 h of alkaline exposure in 1 M KOH at room temperature displayed its exceptional chemical stability. Furthermore, the H2/O2 fuel cell using organic – inorganic hybrid composite membrane formed using 3 wt% of QPOSS relative to QPPO reached a maximum power density of about 288 mWcm−2, higher than that of pristine QPPO membrane. All the results suggested that the prepared organic-inorganic hybrid AEMs are promising for applications in alkaline fuel cells.
